name: Worst-case representation technique for Subset Balancing (Randolph-Wegrzycki)
description: Randolph and Wegrzycki bring the Howgrave-Graham-Joux representation technique from average-case to worst-case inputs for Subset Balancing (find nonzero c in C^n with c.x = 0). Using mixing dichotomies, coefficient shifting and compatibility certificates, they beat the |C|^{n/2} meet-in-the-middle barrier for C=[-d:d] (d>1) and C=[+-d] (d>2), and improve Equal Subset Sum to O(1.7067^n). C={-1,1} (Partition) and C={-2,-1,1,2} remain open.
authors_year_venue: Tim Randolph, Karol Wegrzycki; arXiv:2511.10823 (Nov 2025), 'Beating Meet-in-the-Middle for Subset Balancing Problems'. STOC 2026 venue claimed by the task description but not visible in the arXiv text read [uncertain].
status_and_verification: Preprint (arXiv v1); read via alphaXiv: abstract, Sec 1-2 (technical overview, Fig 1), Lemma 5.1 and Algorithm 2 (Sec 5.2), Sec 6.1-6.2 (coefficient shifting, Lemma 6.1 statement and proof start), Table 1 and Algorithm 3, Sec 7.1-7.2 definitions, Theorem 8.1 statement. Not read: detailed runtime computations (Lemmas 5.2, 6.4, 7.x), Section 8 proofs.
key_theorem_or_bound: Result 1 (Thm 5.1): for C=[-d:d], d>1, worst-case O(|C|^{(0.5-eps)n}), eps=eps(d)>0. Result 2 (Thm 6.1): same for C=[+-d], d>2. Result 3 (Thm 7.1): Equal Subset Sum (C={-1,0,1}) in O(1.7067^n) vs 1.7088^n (MNPW19). Lemma 5.1 (perfect-mixing dichotomy): if two distinct solution pairs of c collide, x admits a 1/(3|C|)-unbalanced solution. Lemma 6.1: if |P_R . x| <= |P(c,C1,C2)| 2^{-eps n} then x has >= 2^{eps n} distinct solutions. Thm 8.1: compatibility pairs found in time O(2^{c(eps)d}(|A|+|B|)). Open: C={-1,1} and {-2,-1,1,2}.
regime_exponents: Exponent below |C|^{n/2} by eps(C) (unspecified constants except worked example [+-3], where the representation algorithm runs in about 2.245^n vs 6^{n/2}=2.449^n on balanced profiles; Table 1 lists d up to 7). Unbalanced solution profiles are handled by folklore meet-in-the-middle (Sec 4). Average-case benchmarks: 2^{0.337n} (HGJ), 2^{0.283n} (BCJ, BBSS). No 0.311n/0.661n statement in the paper; 0.311n and 0.661n are repo/AKKN-context numbers.
proof_type_and_tools: Combinatorial/probabilistic. Representation technique (random prime p, residue r, filter solution pairs). Mixing dichotomies: Lemma 5.1, Lemma 6.1, Lemma 7.2 (either solution pairs mix well, giving the representation algorithm, or an unbalanced or exponentially-many-solutions structure gives another algorithm). Coefficient shifting: write C as sumset C1+C2 (e.g., {0,1}+{-3,-2,1,2}=[+-3]). Compatibility certificates (extending Nederlof-Wegrzycki) to filter pseudosolutions.
quantitative_loss: Exponential gains tiny and non-explicit: eps depends only on C and is unoptimized (computed numerically only for [+-3] and Table 1). Mixing dichotomy trades poor mixing for 2^{eps n} solutions or an unbalanced solution, both exponential-size effects, so the argument is exponential-energy tolerant. Polynomial factors suppressed via O*.
worst_case_vs_average_case: Worst case: all inputs x in Z^n, Monte Carlo with no false positives. This is the point of the paper (vs Chen-Jin-Randolph-Servedio average-case SODA 2022).
coefficient_set: Subset Balancing: C=[-d:d] and [+-d]; includes {-1,0,1} (Equal Subset Sum) and {-1,1} (Partition, open). Standard {0,1} Subset Sum is equivalent to Partition ({-1,1}), which is NOT broken.
subset_size_regime: Solution vectors with a fixed 'solution profile' (frequency of each coefficient); balanced profiles (Theta(n) of each coefficient) are the hard case; unbalanced (deviating by Omega(n)) profiles are solved quickly by meet-in-the-middle. This is exactly the Theta(n)-subset regime.
relevance_to_Nc: Template: Lemma 5.1/6.1 are of the form 'collisions among solution pairs (a.x = a'.x) produce another solution (a-a') with different (unbalanced) profile or exponentially many solutions'. The count of colliding pairs is N_c-like: equal-sum disjoint pairs of Theta(n)-subsets. Bounding N_c for {0,1} would be the missing mixing dichotomy for C=[+-1] where a-a' may have 0 coefficients wherever it should be nonzero (solutions pairs must be restricted to c's support).
relevance_to_Dstar: Mixing is equivalent to the number of distinct dot products a.x over solution pairs being large (about |P(c)|), which is exactly a statement about many distinct half-sums (D* big). Poor mixing (few distinct half-sums) is converted into either an unbalanced solution or many solutions; this is the direct template for C2 (hard instances cannot have few distinct balanced half-sums D*), but the paper proves nothing for {0,1} and no 2^{0.311n} threshold.
applicability_gap: Fails for C=[+-1]/Partition: with no 0 coefficient, the difference a-a' of two colliding pairs may vanish at positions where c is nonzero, so it is not a valid solution (the authors note Lemma 5.1 does not apply) and coefficient shifting needs a decomposition C1+C2 with representation multiplicity (for {-1,1} the sumset factors give no overlapping representations). Also eps(C) is unspecified, and the dichotomy has a different escape ('many solutions') than the repo's D* escape.
counterexample_or_hard_instance_family: No explicit hard family; worst-case instances are those where all solutions are balanced profiles and pairs mix poorly. Equal-Subset-Sum hardness occurs at profile pi(-1)+pi(1) approx 0.773n (MNPW19, giving 1.7088^n). For Partition, hard instances for MITM in the average case: random density-1 (solved by HGJ at 2^{0.337n}, but worst-case unknown).
dependency_chain: AKKN (bin-size dichotomy) and BSG/PFR for structure; Randolph-Wegrzycki (this) supplies the mixing dichotomy template; compose: unbalanced -> MITM, poor mixing -> many solutions/structure, good mixing -> representation. Builds on HGJ, BCJ, MNPW19, CJRS22, Nederlof-Wegrzycki compatibility certificates.
constructiveness: Fully algorithmic: Monte Carlo, success amplifiable to 1-2^{-Omega(n)}; compatibility certificates solve the pseudosolution filtering in near-linear time in list size times 2^{c(eps)d}.
lean_formalizable: Moderate: Lemma 5.1 (pigeonhole/difference-of-pairs argument) and Lemma 6.1 are elementary combinatorics and could be formalized in a mathlib-free setting; the runtime analysis with entropy functions and prime density is heavy.
computational_check: Source reports no experiments; it computes exponent values for [+-3] to [+-7] analytically. Repo scripts (coefficient_shifting.py, bcj_*.py, collision_amplification.py already exist) could check mixing dichotomy lemmas at n<=40 for small d by brute force.
next_experiment: Test the mixing dichotomy for C=[+-1]: for random and structured {0,1} instances with n<=30, enumerate solution-pair collisions of a balanced solution (a.x=a'.x with a != a') and count how often a-a' is a valid disjoint-pair relation vs invalid because it has zeros on supp(c); report the fraction (the quantity that blocks the dichotomy).
open_issues: Partition ({-1,1}) and {-2,-1,1,2} not resolved; eps(C) not optimized; STOC 2026 acceptance not verified from the text; whether the same mixing dichotomy can be proved for balanced solutions of Partition is the main open step for C1/C2.
